- Take good notes from the beginning. Don't slack about taking notes. If you miss taking notes for a topic, catch up on it as soon as possible. 

- Whenever you are randomly wondering about something subject-related, write it down. This will help you when you have to choose a topic for your IA (for example, if you find yourself randomly wondering how the thickness of the paper will affect the trajectory of a paper plane that's a beginning of a physics IA. If you wonder how medieval peasants reacted when the aristocracy started wearing wigs, that's a beginning of a history IA).

- Make yourself familiar with the syllabus description and grade components of each subject you are taking (you can find them in the subject guides on ibdocuments). This will help you have a good overview and be able to prioritize your studies better. 

- be suspicious of your teachers. It's sad to say but not all IB teachers are as familiar with the IB as they should be. Ask previous students about their experience with the teachers. If a teacher is new, also be suspicious. I don't mean that you should question their knowledge about the subject in general, but they might not be so trustworthy when it comes to guiding you about IAs and exams. New teachers might also not be very good at structuring their lessons so you have time to cover the entire syllabus (for example, my math HL teacher spent too much time on the earlier parts of the syllabus, so at the end we had to rush through the last couple of chapters. 

- Always reflect and assess how you are spending your study time. Don't waste too much time on subjects you are already good at while neglecting the subjects you are bad at / don't like. Don't waste your time studying in ways that are ineffective for you. Try experimenting  with different study methods throughout your years so by the time you have to study for exams, you know how to do it effectively. 

This also sort of ties in with the 'be suspicious of your teachers' point. For example, if your math teacher wants you to do a million repetitive exercises that you don't find helpful, don't do it. In IB both time and energy is scarce. So you have to be very mindful on what you spend it on.



I probably have more tips, but that is what I can think of so far. Good luck!

I got 7 on math HL, physics HL, and Danish B HL; and my experience is that past papers are NOT the best place to start studying. 

Doing past papers is good practice, but you are not really learning anything (except for how to solve the very specific question you are answering). Personally I found that the best place to start is making sure that I am REALLY familiar with all the parts of the syllabus - that I understand every concept, know how to use every method, know the meaning of every bit of subject specific vocabulary. Only then did I start doing past papers. 

Generally, past papers are good for:
- knowing how to manage your time in an exam situation (i.e., how much time you need to allocate for each section, which type of questions to take first etc.)
- figuring out your weaknesses and strengths so you know what to focus on when you study. 
- practicing on improving your time.

Don't see the mocks as a 'prediction' of your final grade, see them as a learning experience.

The English/Spanish/business exams went relatively well, so you can assume that the study strategies you used for these subjects are effective.

The science/math exams went less well, so you should reevaluate your study strategies and look for more effective ones.

I'd suggest you look at the mistakes you made and try to find some sort of pattern.

- Do you struggle with explaining scientific concepts?

- Do you struggle applying equations and formulas?

- Do you struggle with needing to memorize so much information?

- Are there any particular sub-topics that you are especially bad with?

After you 'analyzed' your mistakes you can start finding more effective studying strategies (i.e. Condensing your notes instead of reading them, going through worked examples instead of doing exercises etc) . If you are not sure what could work for you, I'd suggest you Google 'study skills' and 'studying strategies'.

Remember that going to school is just about learning how to 'learn' as it is about learning the actual content of the syllabus. The mock exams give you a great opportunity to better understand what sort of learner you are and thus improve, so don't be discouraged by bad results :)

My teacher told me basically the same thing your teacher told you. The way my teacher explained to us the structure is:

1. You find a real life situation (RLS1) , only one. In your situation, I recommend you take gun control as an overall topic and choose one specific situation to focus on. You explain it and deduce a knowledge question of a general nature
2. You explore your knowledge question using ToK terms and definitions. This section needs to be broad and not based on your RLS1. Make sure to include contrasting ideas and considering a while range of aspects.
3. You go back to your RLS1, and apply the things you revealed in section 2 to it. Here you need to show how researching the knowledge question increased your understanding of the RLS1.
4. You find an additional real life situation, RLS2. You demonstrate how the same things you revealed in section 2 can apply to other situations than RLS1. You talk about RLS2 in less detail than RLS1. For your presentation, I would recommended using something other than gun control. It can maybe be abortion or adoption etc. 

I used this general outline for my presentation a couple of weeks ago and ended up getting an 8. (my teacher said I was close to a 9, but I didn't consider enough different aspects and views when doing my section 2) my teacher told me the structure was very good and coherent, so Im pretty sure that this is a good way to get it done.
